title: Talking about the past
goal: Talk about yesterday — and discover that Estonian **has no future tense at all**.
bekal: form the past tense with the infix **-si-** and recognize ten irregular forms
negate past sentences with *ei* + the **-nud** form
talk about the future without learning a single new form

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Nädalavahetus Tartus
dialogs.intro: Monday morning. Kerli asks Budi how his weekend was.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Really good! I went to Tartu.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.id: Really? Who did you go with?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: On my own. I took the bus.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.id: And what did you do there?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ma jalutasin vanalinnas ja käisin muuseumis.
lines.id: I walked around the old town and went to a museum.
lines.literal: I walked-I old-town-in and went-I museum-in.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jah, see oli väga ilus. Ma tegin palju pilte.
lines.id: Yes, it was beautiful. I took lots of pictures.
lines.literal: yes, it was-it very pretty. I made-I many pictures-part.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ma ei teadnud, mis see on. Nüüd ma tean.
lines.id: I didn't know what it was. Now I know.
lines.literal: I not knew, what it is-it. now I know-I.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pole hullu. Aga järgmine kord ma küsin enne.
lines.id: It's fine. But next time I'll ask first.
lines.literal: not-is bad-part. but next time I ask-I before.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Tark otsus. Millal sa jälle lähed?
lines.id: Wise decision. When are you going again?
lines.literal: clever decision. when you again go-you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Järgmisel kuul. Eesti keeles pole tulevikku, eks?
lines.id: Next month. Estonian has no future tense, right?
lines.literal: next month-in. Estonian language-in not-is future-part, right?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ei ole. Sama nagu indoneesia keeles.
lines.id: No, it doesn't. Just like Indonesian.
lines.literal: not is. same as Indonesian language-in.

notes: ⚠️ **Estonian has no future tense.** *Ma lähen* means "I go" **and** "I will go". The time word decides: *ma lähen homme* (I'm going tomorrow), *ma lähen praegu* (I'm going now). English does this too — "I'm leaving tomorrow" — and it means one big chapter you don't have to learn at all.

**Käisin** comes from *käima* — "I've been there". Tell it apart from *läksin* (*minema*): *käisin Tartus* means you went and came back; *läksin Tartusse* means you set off for there. English handles this with "been" versus "gone"; Estonian uses different verbs.
**Kellega** = *kes* + **-ga**, "with whom". Question words take endings too: *millega* (with what), *kellele* (to whom), *kelle* (whose), *millal* (when).

⚠️ **Verivorst** is pork blood sausage, a Christmas dish that turns up everywhere between November and January. If you have dietary restrictions, learn the name — it's rarely translated on English menus.

grammars.title: The past tense — the infix -si-
body: Take the verb stem, insert **-si-**, then add the person endings you already know from unit 10.
after: ⚠️ The third row loses its *-i*: *elas*, not "elasi". It's the only quirk in an otherwise regular pattern.
The second and sixth rows are **identical** (*elasid* for "you" and for "they"). Context always tells them apart; don't worry.

⚠️ Notice *õppisin* has **pp**, while the present *õpin* has **p**. Consonant gradation works differently in the two tenses. Once again the fix isn't a rule — just learn the past form together with the present.

grammars.title: Negating the past — ei + the -nud form
body: Just as in unit 11, *ei* doesn't change for anyone. Only the verb form changes, and that form is the **same** for all six persons.
after: The **-nud** form is also used for "have done": *ma olen käinud Tartus* (I've been to Tartu), *kas sa oled söönud?* (have you eaten?). So it's worth learning for two jobs at once.
⚠️ *Polnud* is short for *ei olnud*, matching *pole* for *ei ole*.
*Kas sa oled söönud?* is very common small talk among Estonians — rather like "have you eaten?" as a friendly greeting in many Asian cultures.

blocks.text: These verbs come up constantly, and their past forms can't be guessed. Memorize the second column; it's the one you'll need most.

blocks.title: ⚠️ How Estonian talks about the future
items: **No special form.** The present tense covers both, as in "I'm flying tomorrow".
*Ma lähen homme Tartusse.* — I'm going to Tartu tomorrow. The word *homme* marks the time.
For extra emphasis, add *hakkan* (will start): *ma hakkan õppima* — I'm going to start studying.
For intentions, use *kavatsen* (intend): *ma kavatsen minna* — I intend to go.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice *ma ei ole veel söönud* — "I haven't eaten yet". Estonian has no single word for "not yet"; it uses *ei ... veel*, just like English "not ... yet". Same pattern: *ma ei tea veel* (I don't know yet), *ta ei ole veel tulnud* (he/she hasn't come yet).

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers.0: Ma elasin Tallinnas. — Sa õppisid eesti keelt. — Ta läks kooli. — Me sõime kohvikus. — Te tegite tööd. — Nad tulid koju.
answers.1: Ma ei olnud kodus. — Sa ei läinud Tartusse. — Ta ei teinud seda. — Me ei söönud. — Te ei teadnud. — Nad ei tulnud.
answers.2: Mida sa eile tegid? — Ma ei teinud midagi. — Ma käisin Tartus. — Kas sa oled söönud? — Ma ei ole veel söönud. — Homme ma lähen Tartusse.
answers.3: Ma käisin Tartus. — Mida sa eile tegid? — Ma ei teinud midagi. — Kas sa oled söönud? — Homme ma lähen Tartusse.
